The idea: **two magic twin coins** — whenever you flip them, they always land the same way (both heads or both tails, never one of each). That's a **Bell state** — two qubits entangled so their measurement results are perfectly correlated.

steps.content:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorSampler

qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)          # 2 qubits, 2 classical bits
qc.h(0)                            # put coin 0 into superposition (spinning)
qc.cx(0, 1)                        # entangle: coin 1 copies whatever coin 0 decides
qc.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])         # flip both coins and record results

sampler = StatevectorSampler()
job = sampler.run([qc], shots=1000)
counts = job.result()[0].data.c.get_counts()
print(counts)

steps.text:
Here's what was built and what it means:

---

### [`recordings/work/twins.py`](recordings/work/twins.py)

```
{'00': 492, '11': 508}
```

**The two twin coins** — out of 1000 flips, they landed **heads-heads (`00`) about 492 times** and **tails-tails (`11`) about 508 times**. The combination `01` or `10` (one heads, one tails) **never appeared** — the coins are magically linked.

Here's how the circuit works:

| Gate | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`H`](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/api/qiskit/circuit#quantum-circuit-model) on qubit 0 | Sets coin 0 spinning — it's neither heads nor tails yet |
| [`CX`](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/api/qiskit/circuit#quantum-circuit-model) (CNOT) on (0 → 1) | Entangles coin 1: *"whatever coin 0 lands, I'll land the same"* |
| `measure` | Forces both coins to land — instantly, always together |

This is the **Bell state** Φ⁺, the simplest form of quantum entanglement. No matter how far apart the two coins are, they always agree.

---

> 💡 **Beginner tip:** Notice we used `QuantumCircuit(2, 2)` — two qubits **and** two classical bits. A common slip is writing `QuantumCircuit(2)` (no classical bits), then getting an error when you try to measure, because there's nowhere to store the result!
